summary: Defines the protocol for the L4S network service. It uses an Explicit Congestion Notification scheme at the IP layer that is similar to classic ECN but gives much more frequent signals, matched to scalable congestion control. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable throughput (L4S) uses ECN marks to tell a sender about congestion more frequently than classic ECN. The sender must use a congestion-control method that reacts safely, while network nodes distinguish L4S packets from classic traffic.

questions: what is the l4s ecn codepoint
how does l4s ecn differ from classic ecn
what is a scalable congestion control
subtitle: An ECN marking protocol that distinguishes L4S traffic from classic traffic.

tldr.problem: Classic congestion signals can create queue delay, while scalable congestion control needs frequent, fine-grained feedback to keep queues short.
tldr.mechanism: L4S senders mark eligible packets with ECT(1); network nodes classify those packets for L4S treatment and signal congestion with CE marks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines an Experimental ECN protocol and lists open questions that the L4S experiment is intended to investigate.

today: RFC 9331 is Experimental. Its text identifies open questions and issues for investigation as part of the L4S experiment.

sections.title: Congestion Signals for Lower Delay
sections.content:
Queues build when traffic reaches a bottleneck faster than the link can send it. Classic congestion control can create variations in the queue as it probes for capacity, which adds delay even when the link remains in use.

L4S pairs scalable congestion control with more frequent network signals and finer sender adjustments. This RFC specifies how packets identify L4S treatment and what senders and network nodes must do with that identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: L4S aims to keep queues short while still using available link capacity. It does this by giving a sender frequent congestion signals and requiring smaller, scalable responses.

sections.title: The ECT(1) Packet Identifier
sections.content:
A sender that wants L4S treatment sets the ECN field in the IPv4 or IPv6 header to the ECT(1) codepoint. The RFC chose ECT(1) and CE as a compromise among requirements for an identifier that is visible at the IP layer and can work across transports.

A scalable transport needs sufficiently detailed feedback about CE marks and must respond to congestion in a way that can coexist with classic congestion controls. It must also be able to fall back to classic congestion control when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender marks L4S packets with ECT(1) in the IP header. The sender must also report congestion marks accurately and respond safely when the network becomes crowded.

sections.title: How Network Nodes Treat Packets
sections.content:
A network node that supports L4S classifies ECT(1) packets for L4S treatment. It also treats CE-marked packets as L4S by default, unless an allowed classifier can identify them as classic traffic.

An L4S queue can mark ECT(1) packets with CE as congestion increases. During persistent overload, the node must drop L4S traffic until the overload subsides and must also provide a classic AQM treatment for classic packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use ECT(1) to recognize packets asking for L4S treatment. They mark packets with CE when congestion rises and must retain a separate treatment for classic traffic.

sections.title: Tunnels and Open Questions
sections.content:
The RFC says L4S generally uses existing ECN tunnel and encapsulation behavior, while identifying a case that needs careful configuration. It also records open questions and issues for the experiment, including coexistence and the conditions under which the intended treatment works.

The specification is Experimental. It defines the packet identifier and behavior around it, while separate documents define congestion-control algorithms and active queue management methods.
sections.plainLanguage: L4S has rules for tunnels and for coexistence with classic traffic, but the RFC leaves questions for experimentation. Other specifications define the particular sender and queue algorithms.
